# Milo — full documentation

Documentation from the main branch. The pinned release may not include every feature described here.

## Install

The [v0.1.7 release](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/releases/v0.1.7.md) is available for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 13 or later. Install it with Homebrew:

```sh
brew install mcc0x/milo/milo
```

Without Homebrew, download and run the installer from the release tag:

```sh
curl -fsSLo milo-install.sh https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/releases/download/v0.1.7/install.sh &&
  sh milo-install.sh
```

The script verifies the release binary against its SHA-256 checksum and installs it to `~/.local/bin` by default. It does not need Rust or Git. If you already installed with Homebrew, run `brew upgrade mcc0x/milo/milo`. If you use the Rex integration, run `milo setup --repair` after upgrading. See [setup and removal](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md) for source installation and uninstall instructions.

From a shell in your project, run `milo` to pick a local pane, or `milo outline` to go straight to the file tree. Press `Enter` on a file to read it, `e` to edit working text, `Ctrl-S` to save, and `q` while reading to go back. No Rex installation, browser, account or setup is needed. In Rex, use `milo setup` if you want the panes arranged beside your shell.

## Workspace settings

Run `milo web` in your project to open the [settings dashboard](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#browser-editor). It’s built into the CLI and uses the same settings as `milo setup`. No account, Node.js, or separate install is needed.

Choose a pane layout for one worktree or set a global default. Under **Integrations**, you can have Rex arrange new shell tabs, forward alerts to Discord or Telegram, or show Discord presence. To configure [another Rex host](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#several-rex-hosts), run `milo web --host HOST`.

[Alert forwarding](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#mirror-rex-alerts) reconnects when Rex returns, but an explicit pause stays paused. Lifecycle notices are optional for each destination. A separate opt-in adds a verified Rex session label to ordinary alerts. Both choices are off by default.

<p align="center"><img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-settings.webp" width="760" alt="Milo settings for the tidebook worktree. The Integrations page shows Rex automation, Discord presence and alert forwarding, all off."></p>

## Outline

<p align="center">
  <img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/outline.png" width="570" alt="Project files with colours and line counts for changes to commit or push">
</p>

See changed files in the project tree as you work. Bold colours mark changes to commit; regular colours mark changes to push. Press `/` to find a file by name or path, and `Enter` to read it.

## History

<p align="center">
  <img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/history.png" width="570" alt="Recent commits, with the newest commit open to show its changed files">
</p>

See recent commits and, when the branch tracks a remote branch, how many still need to be pushed. Press `Enter` on a commit to see the files it touched, then on a file to read that version.

## Usage

<p align="center">
  <img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/usage.png" width="860" alt="Codex and Claude Code limits showing percent left, time until reset and an Opus weekly limit">
</p>

See how much of each reported limit you have left. Milo reads local reports saved by oh-my-pi, Codex and Claude Code, and the tokens and estimated cost OpenCode recorded today. It shows the tools that have a figure on this Mac, so there is no empty place for one you do not use, and setup can always show or hide each tool. Where the terminal can show pictures, such as in Rex, the pane can draw the logos and large figures as pictures.

### In the macOS menu bar

Keep an eye on usage without switching to Rex. **Milo** shows the mascot beside your lowest fresh remaining percentage by default. Click it for reset times, switch to **CPU** or **Memory** under **More options → Menu bar indicator**, or choose **Browser settings…** to open the browser editor.

<p align="center"><img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/menu-bar.webp" width="312" alt="Milo’s macOS menu showing example Codex and Claude Code limits, reset times and a Settings button"></p>

On an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS 13 or later, run `milo menubar install`. The Homebrew and release binaries include the app; it only runs if you install it. See [menu bar setup and removal](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/usage.md#macos-menu-bar).

## Discord presence

Optionally show **In a Rex session** on your Discord profile, under Milo's name and icon, while a Rex app has a session open. It is off until you turn it on with `milo presence enable`, in Settings or in the browser editor, and each of them says what becomes public first. Nothing about your sessions, projects, files or commands is sent unless you also choose to show the name of the session in front, its Git project's folder name, or both. No bot, token or sign-in is involved, and you can use a Discord application of your own instead of Milo's. See [Discord presence](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md) for setup, privacy and limits.

## Reader

<p align="center">
  <img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/reader.png" width="675" alt="A TypeScript file with coloured code and green and red lines showing edits">
</p>

Read a file with added and removed lines marked, or open it as it was at a commit. Press `n` or `N` to jump between changed blocks, or `c` to fold unchanged stretches. In Rex, files opened from the same Outline or History pane share one floating reader as [tabs](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#tabs-in-the-floating-reader). The reader colours [about thirty languages](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#languages), from Rust and TypeScript to Markdown, HTML and CSS.

The working-file Reader can also [view pictures, play supported MP4s, and render Markdown](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#reading-pictures-video-and-markdown). On a verified local Mac, press `Ctrl-O` on a working document in Outline, Find or Reader to open it in its default app, or `Ctrl-R` to [reveal it in Finder](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#opening-a-file-outside-milo-on-a-mac).

Press `e` to edit a working text file where you are reading it. The edit is a draft until you save with `Ctrl-S`, and a save never replaces a file that changed on disk without asking. `Ctrl-F` formats the draft with a [formatter you have installed](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#formatting); `Ctrl-Z` takes it back. See [editing files](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#editing-files).

To review an agent’s edits without mixing in your own uncommitted work, have it hand you its recorded patch and run `milo review PATCH`. In Rex, `--float` opens that [read-only review](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#reviewing-an-agents-edits) over the current tab. Milo checks that the patch still fits, not who wrote it.

## What works in each terminal

| Command or feature | Ordinary terminal, no Rex | What Rex adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `milo` (Home) | Choose Outline, History, Usage or settings. No first-run guide on this path. Quit a pane to return to Home. | The existing settings and maintenance Home, with a first-run guide. |
| `milo outline [DIR]` or `milo DIR` | Browse and search a plain folder or Git worktree; open a file in place. | Managed sidebar, floating reader tabs, optional shell-following and temporary outline peek. |
| `milo history [DIR]` | Browse Git commits, expand a commit and read its file at that revision in place. | Managed sidebar and floating reader tabs. |
| `milo view FILE` / `--edit` / `--commit ID` | Read in the current terminal. Edit a working text file; save explicitly. A commit is read-only. | Same direct command. |
| `milo review PATCH [--from NAME]` | Read a handed-over patch in place. | `--float` can open the review from a non-interactive caller in a Rex pane. |
| `milo usage` / `usage --menu-stream` | Show available local figures in a pane, or emit a stream for the menu app. No provider sign-in required. | Optional compact Usage rail. |
| `milo setup` | Terminal settings, including icon, Git mark and usage choices. The explicit command offers a skippable first-run guide. | Try, save, repair or remove managed layouts. |
| `milo web [--no-open]` | Local settings dashboard. `--no-open` prints a private loopback link instead of opening the browser. | `--host HOST` uses Rex to forward **another** host’s editor. |
| `milo settings export GROUPS` / `import FILE [--apply]` / `undo` | Transfer selected settings as a file. Import previews unless you ask to apply. | Saved rail geometry can be used by a Rex layout. |
| `milo doctor`, `--help`, `--version` | Plain output; no TTY needed. Doctor distinguishes local preferences from optional integrations. | Reports Rex host and integration health. |
| `milo alerts`, `milo presence` | Inspect the settings without a running session. | Actual event mirroring and activity presence require Rex and explicit opt-in. |
| `milo listen`, arrange/remember rails, title tabs | Not standalone features. Run a direct pane command instead. | Managed by the Rex integration. |
| `milo menubar install` / `uninstall` / `indicator` | Optional on macOS with a menu-enabled build; choosing an indicator does not install the app. | Not Rex-dependent. |
| `milo claude-status` | Status-line helper for an explicitly configured Claude Code profile, not an interactive pane. | Not Rex-dependent. |

`milo setup --skip-onboarding` records a skip without opening a TUI or applying settings. Direct pane commands never run the guide. See [Using the panes](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md) for input and display fallbacks, and [terminal checks and measurements](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/evidence/terminal-portability/README.md) for the environments actually exercised.

# Set up milo

![Milo’s layout picker with the project sidebar selected beside its split preview](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/setup.png)

## Install

The [v0.1.7 prebuilt release](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/releases/v0.1.7.md) is for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 13 or later. Use Homebrew:

```sh
brew install mcc0x/milo/milo
```

Or download the versioned release installer from GitHub:

```sh
curl -fsSLo milo-install.sh https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/releases/download/v0.1.7/install.sh &&
  sh milo-install.sh
```

The installer checks the binary against a pinned SHA-256 checksum before placing it in `~/.local/bin`. Set `MILO_BIN_DIR` to choose a different directory. The prebuilt installer does not need a compiler, Cargo or Git.

To upgrade, run `brew upgrade mcc0x/milo/milo` for a Homebrew install, or download and run the new version’s installer for a script install. If you installed the Rex integration, run `milo setup --repair` after upgrading so Rex loads the current actions and listener. If you installed the macOS menu app, run `milo menubar install` again to update it.

To build from source instead, install Git and Rust 1.91 or later, then run:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/mcc0x/milo.git
cd milo
sh install.sh
```

The source installer builds the checkout containing the script, even when launched from another directory. A standalone or piped copy clones Milo from GitHub into a private temporary directory instead.

The source installer also honours `MILO_BIN_DIR` and defaults to `~/.local/bin`.

Current installers write a receipt for the binary and its install path. Use a current installer with `--uninstall` and the same `MILO_BIN_DIR` to remove it. If the binary has changed or the receipt is missing or invalid, the installer leaves the binary in place. Older installs may not have a receipt; verify the binary before removing it manually rather than running an older installer’s `--uninstall`.

## Without Rex

From the directory you want to browse, run `milo outline`, `milo history` or `milo usage`. Use `milo view FILE --edit` for a working text file. Or run `milo`, choose a pane with the arrow keys and `Enter`, and return to the picker with `q` after closing the reader. Standalone Home does not record a welcome choice or install anything.

Choose **Terminal settings** for local preferences; you do not need to arrange a layout to save them. To use the browser editor without launching anything externally, run `milo web --no-open` and open its private link yourself. See the [command and feature matrix](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/README.md#what-works-in-each-terminal).

## In Rex

In a Rex shell run `milo setup`. Pick **Just the tree**, **Project sidebar**, or start from the tab you already arranged. Adjust the individual panes and appearance if needed. Trying the layout does not change your saved default; undo the trial before saving if it isn't what you want.

In Home, the welcome guide and Settings, moving the pointer over a clickable control underlines it without changing your keyboard selection. **Click once** to open a menu, switch sections or change a value. Click **Save** and choose a scope to keep your changes. Terminals without mouse-motion reporting still support the arrow keys and Enter.

In narrow Settings panes, rows use shorter labels. When there's room, the full name and value of the selected setting appear below the list.

**Unsaved changes** stays visible while you edit. If you leave Settings from Home or `milo setup`, choose **Save**, **Discard**, or **Keep editing**. Save asks for a scope for each changed group: layout, then appearance and workflow together. Claude Code choices apply to the active profile and do not need a scope. Each confirmed save takes effect as you go, so going back does not undo changes you have already saved. Leaving also undoes any layout trial you haven't kept by saving it.

Save for **this worktree** to keep a project-specific setup, or save a **global default** for projects without an override. Worktrees of the same repository can have different choices. Preferences live on the machine running Milo, outside the repository. A project cannot install actions or supply a command for Milo to execute.

If the saved layout changes while Settings is open, Milo keeps the newer layout instead of overwriting it. Reopen Settings to edit that layout.

Saving appearance or workflow preferences changes only the settings you edited. A worktree still inherits global values for any settings it does not override, and saving global defaults does not copy worktree overrides.

If a worktree's preferences file is unreadable or invalid, panes keep using global preferences. If the global file is broken, panes use built-in defaults. Milo leaves the files alone and shows a notice; run `milo doctor` to find the file and the error, then correct it and reopen the panes.

Usage starts as a two-row strip in the shared sidebar. Drag a divider in an installed Milo sidebar and Milo remembers the proportions for that Git worktree automatically. To save a layout explicitly or make it the global default, use **Milo: Remember This Layout…**. Milo stores pane roles and proportions, not processes or live pane IDs. Mixed rails containing another app are left alone.

![A Rex tab with Outline, History and the compact Usage readout in one rail beside the shell](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/tab.png)

Turn on **Arrange new shell tabs** to apply the layout to new shell tabs, including the first tab of a new session. Save this switch globally; changing it alone does not replace either the global or worktree layout. If Usage is sized in rows, Milo waits for a Rex client to measure the tab, so a background tab may arrange when you first show it. Tabs opened to run a command and tabs with their own layout are left alone. Turn it off and save globally to stop arranging new tabs. The panes also work on their own outside Rex.

Use the appearance choices to preview icons, choose text change marks, and turn animated activity marks off. Usage shows Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode only while each has a figure to show; choose **Always show** or **Hide** for a tool to [decide that yourself](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/usage.md#which-tools-appear). Use the workflow choices to pin Outline and History to the starting project or follow the shell they were opened beside. Milo does not change Rex's font, theme, shortcuts or notification settings.

**After Rex restarts, a sidebar can come back as shells instead of Milo.** The dividers and pane labels survive, but on Rex preview.23 (server API 19) the running programs do not. To restore the sidebar, focus its tab’s working shell and run **Milo: Arrange This Tab** in the Rex app. Milo checks what’s running before it offers to rebuild. New shell tabs are arranged as before.

**Text zoom is separate from split size.** On Rex preview.21 (server API 18), Milo can read a terminal's cell dimensions, but creating or resizing a terminal does not set the font the Mac app renders. The app exposes relative font actions and an app-wide [starting font size](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/mac-settings.md#setting-typography-font-size), not an absolute per-pane zoom setting. Milo therefore remembers divider positions, not text zoom, for Outline, History and Usage.

Inside Rex, run `milo` for Home or `milo setup` to go directly to Settings. Both share the same first-run guide. To skip it in an install script, run `milo setup --skip-onboarding`; it records the skip and exits without requiring a terminal or installing integrations. `milo outline` and the other direct pane commands never show the guide. Terminal panes work without Rex; split geometry and shell-following require Rex.

## Tab titles and session names

Milo leaves tab and session names alone unless you ask. It builds a name from folder names and the name of an agent's process. It never reads what a terminal shows, a terminal's title or a program's status text, so nothing you type to an agent ends up in a name.

Turn on **Title Rex tabs** under **Workflow** in terminal Settings or **Integrations → Rex automation** in the browser to name tabs that nobody has named. A tab is titled after the Git project its shell is in: `project` in the repository's own folder and `project/worktree` in a linked worktree. While Claude Code, Codex or oh-my-pi runs in one of the tab's shells, the title ends with ` · claude`, ` · codex` or ` · omp`. A tab outside a Git project keeps the label Rex gave it. The setting is off by default. Save it globally, or for one worktree to title tabs only there or everywhere but there.

Milo titles a tab only while its label is Rex's own, such as `Window 89abcdef`, or the title Milo set last. Rename a tab yourself, in the app or with `rex window rename`, and Milo stops titling it. Clear the name to hand the tab back. Milo remembers the titles it set by Rex window ID in its state folder, so a name you chose is still respected after Rex or Milo's listener restarts.

New tabs use the current title setting. For an open tab with file-backed preferences, the listener picks up an edit on the next shell or tab-layout event, without polling. Otherwise the title is reconsidered when the directory or foreground agent changes. Turning titles off returns the tab to Rex's label. Agents are recognised by their program name: one started under another name, such as `node`, is not shown.

The listener starts Milo to ask about a directory once, and with titles on once more for each agent that runs there. After that it asks again when your global preferences or that worktree's own have changed, or when a folder outside any project has gained a repository. So with titles off, other tabs in a directory and later visits to it normally start no further process. Milo is asked every time about a directory it cannot vouch for: one outside a project with a folder above it that other users can write to, such as `/tmp`, one reached through a link, or one where Git could not run.

**Milo: Name Session from This Project** renames the session you run it in after the project of its shell: `project`, or `project/worktree` in a linked worktree, without the agent. It is the only way Milo names a session, and it happens only when you run the action: from the command palette, with a key you bound to it, or with `rex do milo_name_session`. It creates no session and switches to none. Outside a Git project it changes nothing and says so. Milo does not remember the name or keep it up to date, so rename the session again whenever you like. The action does not depend on **Title Rex tabs**.

Both need the installed Rex integration. After upgrading Milo, run `milo setup --repair` so Rex loads the current actions and listener.

## Browser editor

Run `milo web` from the project you want to configure, or choose **Open browser settings** from Milo Home. Milo opens the editor through a short-lived private file so it doesn’t pass the session key to the launcher. If the editor doesn’t open, use the private link printed in the terminal. `milo web --no-open` prints that link without opening a browser. The link is printed at once; a page opened from it waits the moment Milo takes to read your settings. Keep the command running while you edit. The page is served by the Milo executable on this machine, not by usemilo.net. No account, network service, or separate frontend install is needed. Don’t share the link.

![The local editor’s Integrations page for an example worktree, with Rex automation, Discord presence and alert forwarding all off](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-settings.webp)

On macOS, the optional [Milo menu app](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/usage.md#macos-menu-bar) also opens this editor from **Browser settings…**. To configure a particular worktree, run `milo web` from that project.

The editor listens on `127.0.0.1:6110` by default. Use `milo web --port 7000` to choose another port, or `--port 0` for an available port when running a second editor.

Use **Layout** for pane order and sizes, **Panes** for Outline, History and shared appearance, and **Usage** for tools, accounts and display. In Rex, the layout actions menu lets you copy the current tab’s layout or try the draft in that tab. Undo a trial to restore the previous layout. Save explicitly for the current worktree or as the global default; Claude Code choices apply to the active profile. Outside Rex you can still edit and save settings.

**Integrations** groups Rex automation, Discord presence and alert forwarding. Rex automation uses drafts; presence and forwarding apply immediately. **Menu Bar** manages the optional macOS app. **Hosts** names the computer these settings belong to and copies settings to or from [another Rex host](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#several-rex-hosts). **Health** checks for problems and shows the host and its Rex version.

After saving, the confirmation names the destination: global defaults, the current worktree, or the active Claude profile. If open panes still use the old preferences, the browser keeps **Reopen panes to apply** in the project bar after the confirmation fades. Editing again clears the reminder.

Terminal Settings and the browser editor check for intervening changes before saving preferences or removing a worktree override. If another editor saved first, reopen the settings and review the current values rather than overwriting them. In terminal Settings, save or discard layout and Claude drafts before repairing or removing integrations.

In **Health**, run a check of saved settings and the live layout. If the original Rex tab is no longer available, Health warns unless it finds a more serious issue. Saving settings or changing the live layout clears the old result; run the check again for an updated verdict.

While the page is open, it periodically keeps the local session alive only if it has unsaved changes, an active layout trial, or queued edits. This does not save your work, and the session can still time out if the browser suspends the page.

**Done** closes the editor only after undoing any active layout trial. If undo fails, the editor stays open so you can retry. Stopping Milo with `Ctrl-C` or letting it time out only attempts to undo the trial. Closing the browser tab alone leaves the private link usable until Milo stops or the session is idle for 15 minutes. When the session ends, unsaved drafts are discarded; saved settings stay as they are.

The dashboard ships inside `milo`: using it needs no Node runtime, account, or internet connection. For UI development, use Node 26 and Bun: `cd dashboard && bun install --frozen-lockfile && bun run dev`. Open the private URL printed in the terminal. Next.js Fast Refresh updates the interface against a real local Milo session. `MILO_BIN` selects the backend executable (default `milo` on PATH); `MILO_PROJECT` selects the project to edit; `PORT` selects the development port (default `6110`). Stop the development server with `Ctrl-C`.

## Several Rex hosts

Each Rex host has its own Milo: its own binary, settings, state and integrations. Nothing is shared or synchronised on its own. Three things make several hosts feel like one setup: Milo says which host you are looking at, you can open another host’s settings from the computer you are using, and you can copy the settings you choose from one host to another. With a single host nothing changes.

Several Rex apps attached to one server, such as a Mac and a phone, are one host: they share one Milo and one set of settings.

### Which host this is

`milo doctor`, **Health** and **Hosts** in the browser editor name the computer Milo runs on, the first part of Rex’s ID for that host, the version and API revision of its Rex server, and whether a Rex app is open on that computer:

```
Host: studio (Rex host d4744373)
Rex server: 0.1.0-preview.23, API 19; rex command: the same
Rex compatibility: checked with API 19. This is the Rex API Milo was checked with.
Rex apps: open on this computer
```

Milo’s Rex files are checked against API revision 19, which is Rex Server & CLI 0.1.0-preview.23. A newer server is noted and is no warning, because Rex keeps older calls working. Health warns in two cases: the server is older than that revision, or the `rex` command and the server are different versions. In the second case, restart or update Rex before saving a layout, because Milo validates its Rex files with the command and the server is what reads them.

Milo acts on the pane it was run in, never on whichever pane has focus. It knows that pane from `REX_BLOCK`, which Rex sets in every terminal, and lets Rex find the session that holds it. Rex before preview.23 also set `REX_SESSION`; where a terminal still has it, Milo uses that session as before.

The computer’s name stays on that computer and in the pages its editor serves. It is not sent to Telegram, Discord or the relay.

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-hosts-mobile.webp">
  <img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-hosts.webp" width="760" alt="The Hosts page of the browser editor on an example computer named studio: its Rex version, API revision and host ID with a Checked mark, the command that opens another host's settings, and the start of Copy settings between hosts">
</picture>

### Open another host’s settings

On the computer you are using, run:

```sh
milo web --host studio                       # a label from `rex hosts`, or an address as for `rex -S`
milo web --host studio --project /home/you/src/app   # that worktree's settings; the path is on the host
```

Milo checks that the host answers, starts `milo web` there in a Rex session of its own named `milo-settings`, and carries it to your computer with `rex forward`. It then prints the private link and opens it. The page says `studio · forwarded` in its session bar, and **Hosts** and **Health** show that host, so you can tell which settings you are editing.

![Health in a forwarded editor: All good, and a card naming the example host buildbox, its Rex version and API, and that these settings were opened from another computer through a Rex forward. The session bar reads buildbox · forwarded](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-health-host.webp)

The protections are the same as for a local editor:

- The editor on the host listens only on the host’s `127.0.0.1`, and the forward listens only on your computer’s `127.0.0.1`. Nothing listens on a network address. Milo waits for Rex to confirm that its forward is listening before opening or printing the private link.
- The host’s editor is told the one address the page will have on your computer before it starts. It accepts that exact `Host` and `Origin` and no other, including its own port on the host.
- Every settings request still needs the session key in the link. Don’t share the link.

**Done** in the page, `Ctrl-C` in the terminal, or 15 minutes without use ends the editor on the host. Milo closes the forward and removes the `milo-settings` session. If the watcher fails or the tunnel closes before the editor confirms it ended, `milo web --host` reports an error and still cleans up locally. If the host cannot confirm remote cleanup, Milo names the session to look for.

The host needs the same version of `milo` on the search path of its login shell, and you need to be able to reach it with `rex -S`. If `milo web` runs on a host where every connected Rex app is on another device, it opens no browser there and prints this command instead.

### Copy settings to another host

Choose what travels. Nothing is exported unless you name it:

```sh
milo settings export appearance,layout --output milo-settings.txt   # or workflow, usage, all
milo settings export all --scope all --output milo-settings.txt     # global defaults and this worktree's own
```

Move the file however you like. On the other host:

```sh
milo settings import milo-settings.txt           # shows every change; saves nothing
milo settings import milo-settings.txt --apply   # makes those changes
milo settings undo                               # takes the last import back
```

The same steps are under **Hosts** in the browser editor: tick the groups, **Create bundle**, paste it into **Import** on the other host, **Preview**, then **Import**. With `milo web --host` you can do both ends from one computer.

![Import under Hosts, in the editor of an example host buildbox opened through a forward: a table of four settings with their values now and after import, a note that four settings already match, and an Import 4 settings button beside Preview](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-hosts-import.webp)

| Group | What it carries |
| --- | --- |
| `appearance` | Icons, Git text marks, static or animated activity marks |
| `workflow` | Project following, changed files only, follow writes, follow new commits |
| `usage` | Whether Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode show, and large figures |
| `layout` | Panes, side, order and proportions of the saved rail |

**What never travels.** Tokens, webhook links, alert destinations, provider account keys and their on/off choices, Discord presence, the menu app, Claude Code status-line setup, **Title Rex tabs**, **Arrange new shell tabs**, the Rex integration files and everything in the state folder. A bundle that names any of these is imported without them, and the preview lists each line it left out. Set those up on each host.

**Projects at different paths.** A bundle holds no path from the host it came from. For a worktree it records the folder name, the folder below your home if it is there, and the ID of the commit the repository’s history starts from. An import applies a project’s settings to a worktree only when that worktree starts from the same commit: the one you run the command in, or the one at the same place below your home. A folder with the same name is never enough. To choose a worktree yourself, use `--map NAME=DIR`, or **Apply to** in the browser preview. A shallow clone has no starting commit to compare, so map it by hand.

**Conflicts.** The global defaults are replaced setting by setting; settings you did not export, comments and unknown lines in the file stay. A layout is replaced whole. An import is all or nothing: if a settings file changes between the preview and the import, nothing is written and you are asked to preview again.

**Undo.** `milo settings undo`, or **Undo import** under **Hosts**, restores exactly the files the last import replaced. If a setting it changed has been changed again since, nothing is undone and Milo says so. Only the last import is kept.

**Limits.** One worktree’s settings travel per export, the one you run it in. Importing a layout saves the layout; it does not install the Rex integration on a host that has none, so run `milo setup` there once. Panes that are open read the new settings when you reopen them. A bundle written by a newer Milo is refused with a request to update.

## Rex actions

Saving installs these actions in the Rex command palette:

| Action | Name for a key binding |
| --- | --- |
| Milo: Arrange This Tab | `milo_layout` |
| Milo: Add the Outline | `milo_outline` |
| Milo: Add the History | `milo_history` |
| Milo: Add the Usage | `milo_usage` |
| Milo: Close Panes in This Tab | `milo_close` |
| Milo: Peek Outline | `milo_peek_outline` |
| Close the outline peek | `milo_close_peek` |
| Remember the current rail | `milo_remember_layout` |
| Reset a remembered layout | `milo_reset_layout` |
| Name the session after this project | `milo_name_session` |

Milo does not install key bindings. For an optional shortcut, check Rex's shortcut settings and `rex keymap` first; the latter lists config bindings, not every Mac app shortcut. If the chord is free, put a binding such as `rex.bind("cmd+shift+m", "milo_peek_outline")` in your own Rex `init.lua`. Actions also work directly in the palette without any binding.

Peek opens a floating outline and takes focus. Invoking it again raises the same peek. Dismiss it to return to the originating pane. Adding the docked Outline instead keeps the shell focused. Your existing custom actions remain yours.

Setup adds two marked lines at the top of `~/.config/rex/init.lua` (after the interpreter line, if it has one) and asks Rex to reload. The actions live in `~/.config/milo/rex.lua`. `~/.config/milo/listener.lua` watches for divider changes even when arranging new shell tabs is off, and titles tabs when you have chosen that. If `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is an absolute path, both folders live there instead. `$REX_CONFIG` can point directly to a different settings file. Milo keeps its saved state in `~/.local/state/milo` or under an absolute `$XDG_STATE_HOME`.

Setup does not rewrite your actions or key bindings. It refuses to change read-only settings files or use a linked milo configuration folder. The settings file itself may be a symbolic link: setup edits the target and keeps the link.

## Claude Code limits

**Show Claude Code limits** adds milo to `~/.claude/settings.json` only if you do not already have a status line. Turning it off removes milo's entry, not one you added yourself. If the option is unavailable because you already have a status line, milo leaves it alone; [other sources](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/usage.md#where-the-figures-come-from) may already provide limits.

If you set `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, Milo uses that profile's `settings.json` instead and tracks its installation separately.

New setups use the full path to Milo, so Claude Code does not need `milo` on its `PATH`. If Doctor reports an old launcher, turn limits off, save, then turn them back on and save.

## Mirror Rex alerts

Milo can send the same Rex alert to Telegram, Discord, or both. Forwarding is off until you enable it. Rex's own tab marks, sounds and notifications stay as they are: Milo listens to `rex events` and changes no Rex setting.

```sh
milo alerts telegram -1001234567890   # asks for the bot's token; or: milo alerts discord
milo alerts                           # what is saved, whether it is running, what would be sent
milo alerts test                      # one message written by Milo
milo alerts on                        # starts, and says again what is sent
milo alerts on discord                # enable just Discord, leaving Telegram as configured
milo alerts on telegram               # now send to both
milo alerts test telegram             # test only Telegram
milo alerts notices on discord        # let Milo announce forwarding changes in this channel
milo alerts notices off discord       # silence those notices, without pausing Rex alerts
milo alerts off                       # ends it at once
```

In `milo web`, open **Integrations → Alert forwarding** to manage destinations, forwarding switches and lifecycle notices. In `milo setup`, **Workflow → Mirror Rex alerts…** controls global mirroring, event kinds and content, and can test a saved destination. Both ask before turning on forwarding. The terminal setup panel never takes a secret: save one with `milo alerts` or the browser editor.

In the browser, choose **Set up destination** (or **Manage destinations**). For Telegram, enter the bot token and look for a chat in its recent updates. If your chat isn’t listed, message the bot there and try again, or enter the chat ID or public `@channel` yourself. Bots already using a webhook need manual entry; Milo doesn’t disconnect their webhook. Looking for chats doesn’t save a destination or turn on forwarding.

Each saved destination has its own forwarding switch and test button. Turn on both switches to send each alert to both places, or test either destination without enabling forwarding. Forgetting one leaves the other connected.

**Lifecycle notices** are optional for each saved destination and off by default. Under **Manage destinations**, turn on **Lifecycle notices** for the chat or channel where you want them. Milo can send a short message there when forwarding is enabled, explicitly paused, or recovers after an interruption. A notice contains only the forwarding state, not the Rex alert, program, host, chat name or reason for the interruption. Milo does not announce each retry. The final pause notice is best effort: turning forwarding off does not wait for the destination to answer. Forgetting or replacing the destination resets its notice choice.

Changing the recipient or replacing its credential turns off forwarding to that provider until you approve it again. Re-saving identical manual credentials leaves forwarding unchanged. If another editor changes what will be sent while confirmation is open, review the updated details. An old preview Telegram credential without a verifiable chat identity must be paired again; Milo will not guess which DM it belongs to.

Alerts use separate credentials for each config directory. The default config directory keeps its existing saved connections. A custom `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `HOME` that previously used a shared credential must reconnect the destination in that profile and turn forwarding back on. Milo cannot tell which old profile approved the shared credential, so it does not copy it into another profile.

If Milo cannot disconnect a saved Telegram credential using the current relay (for example, one from the old production preview), use its original relay if possible. Otherwise, choose **Forget on this host** (or **Forget on “HOST”** in forwarded settings) in Telegram’s destination settings, or run `milo alerts forget telegram --local-only` on the affected host before reconnecting. This stops Telegram forwarding and removes its credential on that host only; it does not revoke the old connection on the relay or change Discord. To revoke all Milo connections to that chat, send `/stop` to Milo’s bot in the original chat while the issuing relay is available.

See the [Telegram recovery screen on a forwarded host](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/telegram-recovery-host.webp) and the [local-only removal confirmation on mobile](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/telegram-recovery-host-mobile.webp).

**Connect with Milo (requires the hosted service).** The official endpoint is `https://connect.usemilo.net`; the settings dashboard still runs on your device. If the service is not available, use manual setup. For Telegram, confirm in a private DM with Milo’s bot. For Discord, authorize a webhook for your channel. Copy the finish code from the bot’s reply or the confirmation page, then paste it **only in the Milo dashboard where you started pairing**. Pasting or selecting browser autofill opens the destination review. If you type the code, choose **Check connection**. Never send the code to someone who shared a pairing link. The destination is saved only when you choose **Save**; forwarding is enabled separately.

Telegram alerts use the relay; Discord alerts go directly from your device to your channel. Manual setup works without the hosted service. For local development or deployment requirements, see the [relay guide](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/hosted/README.md).

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-alerts-mobile.webp">
  <img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/web-alerts.webp" width="760" alt="The Alerts page of the browser editor: mirroring is off, alerts would go to an example Telegram channel, and the page says that only the kind of alert and the program's short name are sent">
</picture>

![The setup screen's Mirror Rex alerts panel: mirroring off, Telegram as destination, the three status alerts on, notifications and bells off, and Kind only as what is sent](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/setup-alerts.webp)

**What counts as an alert.** A program that reports through Rex's [program status protocol](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status) that it is `blocked`, failed (`error`) or finished (`done`); a program that asks for a desktop notification (OSC 9 or OSC 777); and the terminal bell. The first three are mirrored unless you choose otherwise with `milo alerts events blocked,error,done,notification,bell`. Working and idle reports, progress, exits, titles and everything else in a session are never sent, and neither is anything Milo itself shows.

**What is sent.** By default only the kind of alert and the program's short name, such as `Rex: claude-code is waiting for permission`: no text from the program and no session, tab, folder or file name. `milo alerts content text` adds up to 300 characters of the line the program gave Rex, which can name files or quote a prompt. Both the name and that line come from the program, so they are sent marked as code, where neither Telegram nor Discord makes a link, a mention or formatting of them. The line is also cut to one line with every `@` broken, Discord is told to notify no user, role or `@everyone`, and link previews are turned off.

**Which run finished?** Turn on **Include Rex origin label** under **What gets sent**, or run `milo alerts origin on` on the host running Milo. Telegram might then show `Rex: amp finished · release-review` instead of `Rex: amp finished`; Discord adds the same label to its card. The label can reveal a project or task name. It is off on new and existing installations. `milo alerts origin off` removes it without changing program text or pausing forwarding.

Milo uses the full session and block IDs from the [Rex event](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/events) to check that the terminal still belongs to that session on the local host. It uses the session’s name **at lookup time**: a rename can change what you see, and a closed or missing block produces the ordinary unlabeled alert. Two tabs in one session, or sessions with identical names, can still look alike. Rex does not report the originating tab on these events, so Milo does not use tab names.

A label must fit in 64 ASCII characters, start and end with a letter or digit, and contain only letters, digits, spaces, `_` or `-`. From a session named like `project/worktree · codex`, Milo can take just `worktree`, not the path. It omits unsafe or overlong names rather than sending a misleading fragment. It never infers an origin from focus, terminal output, shell commands, prompt text, OSC terminal titles or another host. The existing `content text` choice alone controls whether the program’s own status title and message are sent.

The same label choice applies after a worker or Rex restart. It does not change which destinations are paused. Lifecycle notices are a separate choice per destination: an enabled, paused or recovered notice carries only Milo’s fixed forwarding-status text, never a session label or program text.

If Rex cannot confirm the local server’s identity when Milo subscribes, alerts on that subscription stay unlabeled. Milo tries to verify the host again on the next subscription; it never attaches labels retroactively.

Discord sends one Milo card per alert, with the Milo icon beside the status, inline code for program names and optional text, a localized send time, and a colored edge: amber for attention, red for errors, green for completion, and Milo blue for notifications, bells and connection tests. Telegram keeps its compact text format.

**Destinations and secrets.** For Telegram, create a bot with BotFather, add it to the chat or channel, and give Milo the chat's number or a public channel's `@name`. For Discord, create a webhook in the channel's **Integrations** settings and give Milo its link; only `discord.com` webhook links are accepted. The bot token or webhook link is asked for without being shown, or read from standard input, never taken as an argument. On macOS it is kept in your Keychain; elsewhere in `alerts-secrets` in Milo's state folder, readable only by you. Settings pages show whether a secret is saved, never the secret. Saving a second destination while alerts are being mirrored does not move them: switch with `milo alerts use`. `milo alerts forget telegram` or `forget discord` removes one, and `milo setup --remove` removes both and ends mirroring.

**Once, not twice.** One background process mirrors, whatever number of tabs, panes and Rex apps are open. Rex repeats a status each time a program reports it; Milo sends it when a terminal enters a state or changes what it is waiting for. A terminal's bell is sent at most once in 30 seconds, and so is a notification that repeats that terminal's last one.

Deduplication lasts for one continuous Rex subscription. Changing the label or content setting opens a new subscription. If the program reports the same state again after that, Milo can send it again; it does not replay old events. Changing a disclosure does not reset a destination’s rate limit.

**When things go wrong.** Ordinary alerts are spaced about a second apart and limited to 20 a minute. Milo drops excess alerts and says how many were omitted in the next message. If a destination asks it to slow down, Milo waits and retries the alert if the requested wait is within a minute. A failing destination gets up to three attempts per alert. After a confirmed credential refusal, Milo stops automatic sends to that destination, including notices. Check the connection, then re-save it or turn that provider off and on to retry. A refusal by Telegram does not pause Discord, or vice versa. `milo alerts` reports the last outcome.

**When Rex goes away.** Milo keeps your forwarding choices. One worker listens for fresh events; if it exits unexpectedly, Milo retries it, and if Rex disconnects, Milo waits and reconnects. Repeated failures increase the wait up to 30 seconds. `milo alerts` and Settings distinguish waiting for Rex or retrying the worker from a user pause. `milo alerts off` pauses both destinations, even during a retry. Use `milo alerts off discord` (or `telegram`) to pause just one. Reconnecting Rex or starting the login listener does not undo a pause.

Use **Refresh status** in the browser or `r` in the setup panel to check again without changing forwarding. See [Waiting for Rex and per-destination lifecycle notices](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/alert-forwarding-after.webp) in desktop and mobile Settings.

**Limits.** Mirroring needs `/usr/bin/curl` and follows only the local Rex server. After a machine restart, Milo resumes enabled forwarding when Rex starts Milo’s [saved layout listener](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#in-rex). If the layout integration is missing, disabled, or too old to start the listener, run `milo alerts on` yourself. Rex does not replay alerts raised during an interruption. Rex decides in each app whether to show its own notification (for example only in the background, or not for a muted tab) and does not report that decision, so Milo mirrors what programs reported, not what Rex showed. A terminal's notifications through OSC 99 do not appear in Rex's event stream and are not mirrored.

## Remove milo

The menu app and CLI uninstall separately. If you want both gone, run `milo menubar uninstall` **before** removing the CLI. This stops the app and unregisters launch at login. Skip this step if you want to keep using the menu bar.

If [Discord presence](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md) is on, **Uninstall Milo** in Home turns it off and takes the activity down. Before removing the binary any other way, run `milo presence disable`.

From Home, choose **Uninstall Milo** to review and confirm removal of the CLI and its managed integrations. **Health → Remove integration** and `milo setup --remove` only disconnect the managed integrations; they do not remove the executable. For manual removal:

1. To diagnose a setup before changing it, run `milo doctor`. To fix the managed integration after an upgrade or executable move, run `milo setup --repair` with the binary you intend to keep.
2. Before deleting the binary, run `milo setup --remove` to disconnect the managed Rex and Claude Code integrations. It also ends [alert mirroring](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#mirror-rex-alerts) and removes its saved destinations and secrets. Saved preferences and user-edited files are not an uninstall target. Close any live Milo panes separately.
3. Remove the binary with `brew uninstall milo` if you installed with Homebrew. If you used the release installer, run `sh milo-install.sh --uninstall` with your downloaded copy. If you built from source, run `sh install.sh --uninstall` from the checkout. For either script, use the same `MILO_BIN_DIR` you installed to if you set one. Removing the binary does not change Rex or Claude Code settings or remove milo's saved state.

If Rex cannot reload during removal, Milo still removes the managed files and tells you to restart Rex. If Milo cannot safely remove its Claude Code status line, correct the reported settings problem and retry before deleting the executable.

If you set `XDG_STATE_HOME` when installing the integration, use the same value for repair and removal. Milo won’t guess which listener or Claude settings entry belongs to an installation it can’t verify.

`milo setup --remove` disconnects only the active Claude Code profile. Before removing the binary, repeat it for any alternate profiles where you enabled limits, using the same `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` as when you enabled them.

## Troubleshooting

Choose **Doctor** in Home or **Read diagnostics** in Settings to check the installation. Press `Esc` to go back without waiting for the checks to finish. For a report to copy from the shell, run `milo doctor`.

- **`milo` is not found:** for Homebrew, check that Homebrew is on `PATH`. The scripts put milo in `~/.local/bin` unless you set `MILO_BIN_DIR`. Add the install directory to `PATH`, or run the binary by its full path.
- **Doctor reports a Rex loader conflict, or setup says Milo's Rex lines were moved, copied or changed:** Milo leaves your Rex settings and listener alone. In the Rex settings file named by Doctor, restore a single copy of Milo's original two lines at the top, just after any interpreter line. Then run Doctor again.
- **Doctor reports an unreadable saved layout profile:** restore a known-good copy of the named file, or back it up and move it aside. Then reopen Settings to use the fallback layout or save a new one. Integration repair does not replace layout profiles.
- **A save was interrupted or actions are missing:** run `milo doctor`. It checks the managed `rex.lua` and `listener.lua` on disk separately from the actions Rex has loaded. If it reports an out-of-date managed file, a stale launcher, a pending reload or missing managed actions, run `milo setup --repair` with the binary you intend Rex to use. If Doctor identifies a custom file, review it yourself. The **Health** section in setup offers the same diagnostics, repair and removal.
- **The sidebar opens at a different size:** run `milo doctor` from that Rex tab to compare the saved sidebar width and Usage height with what's live. If the sizes differ, check [Autobalance splits](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/mac-settings.md#setting-splits-focus-autobalance-splits) under **Settings → Interface → Splits & Focus**. If it is on, turn it off, then close and re-add the Milo panes to apply the saved sizes.
- **Another setup is saving:** only one setup can save at a time. Wait for it to finish before retrying.
- **New shell tabs are not arranged:** enable **Arrange new shell tabs** under **Customize panes**, then save globally. The listener is an account setting, not a per-project switch. `milo doctor` checks whether it is actually running.
- **After Rex restarts, the sidebar shows shell prompts:** Doctor can identify when the sidebar contains restored shells. Finish any work in them and run **Milo: Arrange This Tab**. When Milo can verify the shells are idle, **Keep shells** leaves them untouched; confirming **Rebuild sidebar** closes them, discards their input and scrollback, and opens Milo’s panes with the worktree’s layout. Milo won’t type into a shell or automatically rebuild on restart. If it can’t verify the panes or show a confirmation, inspect them yourself, close only shells you no longer need, and run Arrange again.
- **A tab is not titled:** `milo doctor` shows whether **Rex tab titles** is on for this worktree and whether the listener is running. The listener runs while the saved layout has at least one pane or arranges new tabs. A tab with a name of its own is left alone: clear the name in Rex to let Milo title it. For an already-open tab, change shell directories to trigger a fresh title check.
- **Icons appear as boxes:** choose plain symbols or no icons in setup, or override one launch with `MILO_ICONS=plain` or `MILO_ICONS=off`. Choose a Nerd Font in Rex only if you want one for all of your terminals.

---

Source: https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md

# Using the panes

Use a UTF-8, xterm-compatible terminal that supports cursor positioning and an alternate screen. Both input and output must be terminals. Hardware VTs and the Linux text console are not supported; a non-`dumb` `TERM` alone does not establish compatibility. With redirected output, `TERM=dumb` or `TERM=linux`, use `milo doctor`, `milo COMMAND --help` or another text command instead. You do not need Rex or a particular shell.

Outline and History start in the current directory unless you give them a path. Inside a Git repository they use its root, even when you start in a subfolder. In a plain folder, Outline shows just the files and History says it is not a Git project. To outline a directory named like a command, give its path explicitly: `milo ./history`.

If you initialize Git in that folder, open panes pick up the repository and its saved worktree choices without restarting. Switching branches does not erase remembered folder folds or mark the newly visible timeline as newly arrived.

In a managed Rex pane, Follow mode lets Outline and History use the adjacent shell's working directory, even with a coding agent in the foreground and no directory report from the prompt. If the directory is missing, the pane says **Waiting for shell**; if it cannot open the reported folder, it says **Shell folder unavailable**. It keeps showing the last project and names it when space permits. Neither message changes your project preference to Pin. A standalone pane stays in the project where you opened it.
If Git temporarily cannot identify the shell's project, the pane keeps the last project and retries without another `cd`.
If shell tracking itself stops, the notice changes to **Shell tracking unavailable**. Reopen the pane to reconnect.

## What fits in a pane

| Pane | Size | What you see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outline | 7 rows or fewer | A strip of changed files in a Git project, most recently written first, flowed across the width |
| Outline | 52 columns or more | In the tree, the type of change and how many lines each file gained and lost |
| Outline and history | 12 rows or more | A key hint |
| History | 3 rows or fewer | Recent commits without the heading, dots or divider |
| History | 52 columns and 8 rows or more | A row of dots when there is more than one commit |
| History | Narrow | A shorter summary, such as `↑2` for two commits to push or `no tracking` for a branch that does not track a remote branch |
| History | Narrow and focused | The selected commit's subject wraps so you can read it without widening the rail |
| Usage | Narrow | The limiting window takes priority; if its status does not fit, the provider name stays visible |
| Reader | 2 rows | The filename and one line of content; `n` and `N` show the changed line itself |

In narrow History, the wrapped subject uses only the room below a clicked row, so the row stays under the pointer. In a two-row pane, expanding a commit uses the second row for its first file or an empty-commit note. Collapse it to see the subject again.

The outline and history update on their own. While Git checks the project, the panes keep showing the last result and responding to keys. macOS uses file-change notifications. Where the pane needs to watch but notifications are missing, including on Linux, milo checks about every two seconds. See [keys and marks](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/keys.md) for colours and symbols.

In a plain folder, Outline lists the top level and the folders you expand. A partial-listing warning means Milo reached the 50,000-entry limit or couldn't read every entry. In both plain folders and Git worktrees, Outline warns and omits names that aren't valid UTF-8 rather than showing a name that could open a different file.

If Git holds the index lock for more than a moment, Outline, History and the working-file Reader show `Waiting for Git` and pause automatic updates. They update when the lock clears; Milo never removes it.

Untracked files appear before Milo counts their lines. In a wide outline, `?` means the count is not ready, not zero. The outline counts the files in view in small batches as you scroll; a folder shows `?` while any of its new files are still uncounted.

If filtering or folding hides the selected file, Outline keeps the cursor on its nearest visible folder. Press `r` to refresh counts, including offscreen files.

Press `/` and type part of a filename or path to find it without opening each folder. If the tree is showing changed files only, search uses that same filter. Use the arrow keys to choose a result and `Enter` to read it. Press `Esc` to leave the search without losing your place in the tree. [See Outline path search.](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/pane-outline-comparison.webp)

## Comparing commits

History counts commits to push against the branch's tracked remote branch. `no branch tracked` means there is no tracked branch, not that all commits have been pushed. Milo can still use the remote's default branch to mark commits for comparison. `no remote` means the project has no remote configured.

Expand a commit to see its seven-character ID beside the file count. Narrow panes keep that space for the subject instead.

History lists the latest 300 commits. If there are older ones, `G` takes you to the oldest displayed commit, with `Older commits not shown.` underneath when there is room. A subject longer than 4,096 bytes is cut there and ends with `…`.

Expanding a commit that touched thousands of files shows `Reading files…` under it while Git lists and counts them. The pane keeps taking keys meanwhile, and the files appear under their commit when they are ready, wherever the cursor has gone.

<p align="center"><img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/history-reading-files.webp" width="543" alt="History with the newest commit open and Reading files… under it, while the cursor has already moved to the commit below"></p>

A shallow clone has only part of the project's history. If you expand a commit whose parent is beyond the shallow boundary, History says `Shallow history: parent unavailable.` It does not show every file as new. After fetching more history, press `r` to reload. A genuine first commit still shows its added files.

## Reading files

Open a file from the outline or history with `Enter` or a double-click. Inside Rex it opens in a floating reader, and the next file you open from that pane becomes a [tab](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#tabs-in-the-floating-reader) of the same reader. Any shell you split beside the reader stays open. Outside Rex the reader takes over the pane; `q` brings you back.
History catches up with repository changes when you return from a file, keeping that file selected if it is still in the timeline.

### File actions

Press **a** in the Outline tree or while reading a working file. In Find, press **Ctrl-T** instead: letters still go into the query. **Ctrl-A** and clicking **Actions** work in all three views. The menu names its target. Choose a row with the arrows and `Enter`, click the choice, or press `Esc` to go back. `Enter` in the tree and Find still opens Milo's Reader. Open and Reveal keep their [Mac shortcuts](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#opening-a-file-outside-milo-on-a-mac).

**Preview with tkmp** is an explicit alternative for a working Markdown file. In Rex, it opens a split beside the shell; preview another file in the same tab to replace Milo's preview, not your shell or Reader. Milo does not send a commit, a diff or an editor draft to tkmp. Outside Rex, keep reading in Milo. `milo doctor` reports whether it can find the optional executable without running it. Nothing to enable, install or configure in Milo.

In Peek Outline, the preview goes beside the shell even when another pane opened Peek. Dismissing Peek still returns focus to the pane that opened it. If an older saved Rex layout does not identify the shell, save the layout again in Milo setup before previewing from Peek.

Milo looks for `tkmp` in absolute `PATH` directories outside the checkout and current directory. Use a personal directory such as `~/.local/bin` on `PATH` if your shared tool directory is writable by other users. The selected `.md` or `.markdown` file must be regular UTF-8 text, at most 512 KiB when launched, without terminal controls. Links and paths through linked directories are refused.

Use tkmp only with a previewer, document and project you trust. Milo checks the working file before passing its absolute path as one argument. [tkmp](https://github.com/tfcace/tkmp) runs as your user: it watches and reopens the path on save, emits terminal output and renders diagrams through its embedded JavaScript engine. Those later reads and renders are not sandboxed or bounded by Milo. Milo does not load tkmp's Rex plugin or read the clipboard.

#### Using the full pane width with tkmp

Milo passes only the filename, so a tkmp build without width support needs no special arguments. If **your build's `tkmp --help` lists `--max-width`**, you can opt into full width yourself. Put an executable named `tkmp` in a directory you own, such as `$HOME/.local/bin`, outside the project and before the real tkmp on Milo's `PATH`. Use this as its contents, replacing the quoted executable path with the absolute path to your trusted width-capable binary:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
exec "/absolute/path/to/real/tkmp" --max-width 0 "$@"
```

Make the wrapper executable (`chmod 700 "$HOME/.local/bin/tkmp"`). The absolute path avoids calling the wrapper again; `"$@"` forwards Milo's filename as one literal argument, including spaces and shell punctuation. `milo doctor` should report the wrapper's path. No Milo extra-arguments setting is needed. Built-in fit-to-pane support is tracked in [#94](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/issues/94), pending a released version with [the upstream width option](https://github.com/tfcace/tkmp/pull/1).

### Opening a file outside Milo on a Mac

In the Outline tree, highlight a file with the keyboard or a click. In Find, type a query and choose a result with the arrows. Press **Ctrl-O** to open that file in its default app, or **Ctrl-R** to select it in Finder. The same keys act on the **shown working-file tab** in Reader. `Enter` and double-click still read in Milo. The short strip has no cursor: use `/` to choose a file.

These actions use the file on disk, not the text on screen. They do not export a commit, patch or draft. Finish editing before using them. Use Reveal for folders, executable files, scripts, Finder aliases or files with a custom app binding. A missing file, a symlink, or a path through a linked project folder is refused; Milo never substitutes another file or its parent.

Outside Rex, use a direct Terminal.app or Ghostty session in its standard location. A direct iTerm2 session can also qualify, but a separate session server, an unrecognized shell or wrapper, or a multiplexer prevents Milo from confirming the viewer. Inside Rex, exactly one app must be attached to this session over a local connection as the same user. SSH, remote or mixed viewers, and an uncertain result leave the file unopened. Milo checks when you ask for actions and again when opening or revealing; it never copies the file to a client.

### Tabs in the floating reader

A reader with one file looks as it always has. With a second file, a row of names appears above it: the shown tab is bold and has a `×`, and a yellow `*` before a name marks unsaved edits. Opening a file that already has a tab shows that tab; the file as of a commit is a tab of its own, named with the commit. Two files of the same name are shown with their folders.

<p align="center"><img src="https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/reader-tabs.webp" width="887" alt="A reader with three tabs, table.rs shown with its close mark, and main.rs and notes.md each marked with an asterisk for unsaved edits"></p>

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl-N` / `Ctrl-P` | Next or previous tab |
| `Ctrl-W` | Close this tab. While editing with unsaved changes, asks first |
| `q` or `Esc`, while reading | Close this tab |
| Click a name | Show that tab |
| Click `×` | Close the shown tab |

Where every tab is shown and room is left, the right end of the strip names those keys: `^N ^P tabs · ^W close`, or `^N ^P tabs` alone. `?` lists them first.

Each tab keeps its own place in the file, and while it is being edited its cursor, draft and undo history, however long another tab is shown. A tab that was only being read shows the file as it is now when you come back to it. Closing the last tab closes the reader.

In a narrow pane the strip keeps the shown tab and as many neighbours as fit whole. `‹` and `›` at its edges stand for the tabs beyond, with a `*` when one of those has unsaved edits; click an edge to move that way. A pane under four rows tall shows the file without the strip; the keys still work. [See the strip at 34 columns.](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/reader-tabs-narrow.webp)

Tabs belong to one reader, which belongs to the pane that opened it and to that pane's project. Another Rex session, another project's outline and History beside Outline each have a reader of their own. A reader started with `milo view` in a shell takes no tabs. The reader's Rex label is the file it was last asked to show; it does not follow `Ctrl-N` and `Ctrl-P`.

On iPhone, enable [Rex → Settings → Keyboard → Open Keyboard Manually](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/ios-settings#setting-keyboard-open-keyboard-manually) to browse without raising the keyboard. Tap a folder to expand it, tap a file to select it, and double-tap to open it. This setting affects **all** terminal panes on that iPhone, not just Outline. Tap the keyboard button to type in a shell. If the keyboard reopens when you return to a terminal, turn off **Keep Keyboard Open** in the same settings.

For a quick look at the tree, use **Milo: Peek Outline** in Rex. It reuses one floating outline per tab. Close the peek with `Esc` or `q` rather than removing a permanent pane.

`milo view FILE` reads a working file. `milo view FILE --commit ID` reads the version from a commit. Give the file's path as it was in that commit, relative to your current directory or as an absolute path. For example, from `src`, use `milo view main.rs --commit ID`. Milo ignores `.` components and repeated slashes, but rejects `..`. Use a full or abbreviated hexadecimal commit ID, not a branch name or `HEAD`.

Committed-file lookup requires a UTF-8 path. A working file with a non-UTF-8 name can still be read directly, without a Git diff.

The reader shows the whole file with changed lines marked, and colours the languages below. Working files and files at a commit are recognised the same way, by file name, in any letter case. It uses a small scanner, not a full parser. Other files show as plain text, as does a script whose `#!` line names a different language from its extension. The working-file reader will not open a file outside the project through a linked folder.

### Languages

| Language | Files | Coloured across lines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | `.rs` | Nested block comments, strings, raw strings |
| Python | `.py`, `.pyi` | Triple-quoted strings |
| JavaScript, TypeScript | `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.jsx`, `.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`, `.tsx` | Block comments, template strings |
| Go | `.go` | Block comments, raw strings |
| Java | `.java` | Block comments, text blocks |
| Kotlin | `.kt`, `.kts` | Nested block comments, raw strings |
| Scala | `.scala`, `.sc`, `.sbt` | Nested block comments, raw strings |
| Dart | `.dart` | Nested block comments, triple-quoted strings |
| C, C++ | `.c`, `.h`, `.cc`, `.cpp`, `.cxx`, `.hpp`, `.hh` | Block comments, C++ raw strings |
| C# | `.cs` | Block comments, verbatim and raw strings |
| Swift | `.swift` | Nested block comments, multiline and raw strings |
| PHP | `.php` | Block comments, strings, heredocs |
| Ruby | `.rb`, `.rake`, `.gemspec`, `.ru`, `Gemfile`, `Rakefile` | `=begin` comments, heredocs |
| Elixir | `.ex`, `.exs` | Triple-quoted strings |
| Lua | `.lua` | Long comments and long strings |
| Shell | `.sh`, `.bash`, `.zsh` | Quoted strings |
| SQL | `.sql` | Block comments |
| HTML, SVG, Vue, Svelte | `.html`, `.htm`, `.xhtml`, `.svg`, `.vue`, `.svelte` | Comments, tags, attribute values, and the JavaScript and CSS inside `script` and `style` |
| XML | `.xml` | Comments, tags, attribute values |
| CSS, SCSS, Less | `.css`, `.scss`, `.less` | Block comments |
| Markdown | `.md`, `.markdown`, `.mdx` | Fenced code blocks, comments |
| JSON | `.json`, `.jsonc` | Block comments |
| YAML | `.yaml`, `.yml` | Quoted strings |
| TOML | `.toml` | Multiline strings |
| Terraform, HCL | `.tf`, `.tfvars`, `.hcl` | Block comments, heredocs |
| Dockerfile | `Dockerfile`, `.dockerfile` | |
| Makefile | `Makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, `.mk` | |

Every language has its comments, strings, numbers and reserved words coloured. Markup has tag names, attributes and entities coloured instead, and text between tags is left plain. Markdown has headings, list marks, links, inline code, code blocks and quotes coloured; emphasis and tables stay plain, and a code block is one colour whatever language it holds. Ruby and Elixir strings in quotes are coloured one line at a time. Colour never changes the text shown, and the marks for added, removed and changed words are drawn over it.

When a removed line and the added line that replaces it look alike, the reader highlights the words that changed. A word is a run of letters, digits and underscores in any script; text written without spaces, such as Chinese or Japanese, is compared one character at a time. Highlighting only adds emphasis: the text shown is the same with or without it. Lines that share too little, lines with many separate changes and lines whose edits span more than about a hundred words keep only their red or green background, as do the remaining lines of an unusually large diff.

The reader also labels hidden differences next to the text: `[tab]` versus `[4 spaces]`, `[LF]` versus `[CRLF]`, or a mark such as `[zero-width space U+200B]`. It highlights the character affected by a changed mark, including a combining accent. Ordinary edits do not label unchanged whitespace or marks. Use the horizontal scroll keys to reach labels on long lines.

Press `n` or `N` to jump to the next or previous change. The Reader briefly shows your position (for example, `Change 2 of 5`) or `No changes` if there is nothing to jump to. Navigation wraps in both directions.

Press `c` to fold long unchanged stretches, leaving a little context around each change. Click a folded row to read just that stretch, or use `Tab` and `Enter`. Press `c` again to see the full file. [See the same diff in both views.](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/img/pane-reader-comparison.webp)

## Reviewing an agent's edits

`milo review PATCH` shows what a coding agent says it changed, and nothing else. `PATCH` is a unified diff made from a record of the agent’s own edits, not a diff of the whole worktree. The agent *hands it over*; Milo does not work it out.

Each file the patch names is shown as it is now, whole, with only the patch's lines marked as added or removed. Your own uncommitted work in the same file, another agent's edits, and anything staged or not yet known to Git read as plain unchanged lines. A file the patch does not name is never shown. Nothing is compared with a commit, so the review does not depend on what Git calls changed.

```sh
milo review /tmp/edits.patch --from "Claude Code"           # in your terminal
milo review /tmp/edits.patch --from "Claude Code" --float   # from an agent's shell inside Rex
```

`--from NAME` is shown in the heading as `patch from NAME`, with the file's place among the patch's files. `--float` is for a program with no terminal of its own: it opens the review in a floating pane over the Rex tab the program runs in, prints how many files are shown and a `Not shown:` line with the reason for each that is not, and exits. Without `--float` the review opens in the terminal you run it in.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `]` / `[` | Next or previous file of the patch |
| `r` | Read the files again |
| `n` / `N`, `c`, scrolling | As in the reader |
| `q` or `Esc` | Close |

With more than one file, the last row begins with `[ ] files`. In a pane too narrow for the place in the heading, that hint carries it instead, as `[ ] file 2 of 3` or `[ ] 2/3`, and gives up the other keys first.

The review is read-only: `e` says so, and no file is written, in the project or outside it. The patch is read once when the review opens and is not copied or kept. Milo starts no program for it and asks Git nothing but where the project's top folder is, which the patch's paths are relative to.

### What Milo checks, and what it cannot

A patch is a claim. Milo cannot check who wrote a line, and `--from` is a label, not proof. What it does check is that the claim still fits the file: every hunk's lines, as the patch says it left them, must be in the file now, either where the patch says or in exactly one other place. A patch made one edit at a time can name a file several times; those edits are undone last to first, so a line the agent wrote and later rewrote shows once, from its first state to its last.

When a file does not fit, Milo shows the reason in place of the file and no diff at all. It never falls back to the project's uncommitted changes.

| Shown in place of the file | When |
| --- | --- |
| This file no longer holds the lines the patch left… | Someone changed or removed the patch's lines since, or the patch was not made from this file. |
| The patch's lines are in this file more than once… | The lines around an edit changed, and what is left of it matches several places. |
| The patch edits this file, but it is gone. / The patch removes this file, but it is here. | The file's existence contradicts the patch. |
| The patch names a path that is not a file inside the project. | An absolute path, one with `..`, one inside `.git`, or a name Git quoted. |
| This file is reached through a link… / This is a link… | Milo does not follow a link to show a patch. |
| The patch says this file is not text. / This file is not text. | A binary file, or one that is not UTF-8. |
| The patch for this file cannot be read. | A hunk is cut short or is not a unified diff. |
| Too large to show. / Placing this patch in the file would take too long. | A file over 2 MB, or a patch that matches almost everywhere. |

An empty patch, or text that names no file, opens nothing and says why. That is the right outcome when an agent has no record of its edits.

Where the lines next to an edit have changed since, Milo gives up the unchanged lines at the ends of a hunk one at a time and looks for the rest. At least one unchanged line must stay with the edit, and what is left must then be in the file exactly once. An added line whose neighbours have all changed is not looked for on its own: the same text somewhere else in the file would not be the patch's.

### Limits

- The review shows the files as they were when it opened or when you last pressed `r`. It does not follow later edits.
- A patch is at most 2 MB of text and names at most 200 files; a larger one is refused whole. Renames are shown under the new name, without the old one. A hunk with more lines than its header counts makes its file unreadable, which a hand-written patch can run into.
- An agent can hand over a patch that leaves out some of its edits, or includes someone else's. Milo shows what it was given.
- Edits an agent makes through a shell command, a formatter or a code generator are in the patch only if the agent or its harness recorded them.

### Where the patch comes from

Nothing is installed or configured for this, and no agent settings are changed. The [agent skill](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/skills/milo/SKILL.md#show-the-user-your-own-edits) tells an agent how to produce the patch and when to say it cannot.
